definition.text: Policy tools that use markets, prices and other economic signals to give polluters a reason to cut harmful side effects such as pollution.

facts.text: They tackle the market failure of externalities by charging for external costs through taxes, or by creating property rights and a market for using environmental services.
They are also called economic instruments, price-based instruments or new environmental policy instruments.
Examples include environmental taxes, charges and subsidies, emissions trading, deposit-refund systems, eco-labelling laws and property rights; the EU Emission Trading Scheme is one.
They differ from voluntary agreements and from command-and-control rules that dictate performance or technology, though they usually still need some regulation.
David Lloyd George's fuel tax of 1909-1910 may have been the first UK market-based environmental instrument.
Environmental advocates first opposed them, but after successful credit trading in the US lead phasedown they came to support trading, starting with the acid rain allowance market.

title: Taxes versus tradable permits

definition.text: The trade-off between a pollution tax, which fixes the cost of cutting pollution, and a tradable permit system, which fixes the total amount allowed.

facts.text: A transferable permit system sets a cap on pollution and is likely to reach it more cheaply than other means, possibly undershooting it as technology improves.
A tax has no cap: the pollution cut depends on the rate chosen, which can be adjusted until the incentive works best.
Taxes have lower compliance costs than permits but are less reliable at hitting a target quantity.
Tax revenue can be used to cut other distorting taxes, a possible 'double dividend', though less pollution also means less revenue.
Permits can be auctioned or handed out free by grandfathering, and critics say formal emission rights amount to a licence to pollute.

distinct_from: Market-based instruments versus command and control

title: Market-based instruments versus command and control
article: Market-based environmental policy instruments#Market-based vs command and control

definition.text: The comparison between flexible market-based tools and prescriptive rules such as emission standards and equipment requirements.

facts.text: Market instruments do not dictate technology or equal cuts for every firm, giving firms more flexibility.
Command and control is criticised for blocking innovation, though empirical studies show external price changes can induce it.
Command and control may suit cases where regulators lack information, where trading markets are too thin, or where emissions have purely local impacts.

related: Command and control versus economic incentives
contested_note: Critics say command and control stifles innovation, while empirical studies and some analysts see roles where it works better than markets.

title: Public choice

definition.text: The use of economic tools such as rational choice and game theory to study how politicians, officials and voters behave and interact.

facts.text: It stresses that political agents are self-interested and that collective decisions combine many individual choices.
It doubts that government simply maximizes social welfare, modelling officials who may also act for their own benefit, as in the budget-maximizing model of bureaucracy.
James Buchanan described it as 'politics without romance'.
Duncan Black, sometimes called its founding father, laid groundwork for median voter theory in papers from 1948 to 1958.
Its Nobel laureates include Kenneth Arrow, James Buchanan, George Stigler, Gary Becker, Amartya Sen, Vernon Smith and Elinor Ostrom.
Steven Pressman argues it fails to explain key political behaviour, such as why politicians vote against their constituents' interests.

contested_note: Critics argue public choice cannot explain why people vote or many choices politicians make.

definition.text: The idea that political decisions can produce inefficient policies, much as markets can fail, often because of organized special interests.

facts.text: A small, well-organized interest group can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole.
Because costs are spread thinly and benefits concentrated, vocal minorities with much to gain are heard over indifferent majorities.
Public choice theorists study regulatory capture, pork-barrel spending and logrolling as examples.

definition.text: The theory that a self-interested voter may sensibly choose not to vote or get informed, because one vote almost never decides an election.

facts.text: Anthony Downs argued in An Economic Theory of Democracy that for many citizens rational behaviour means investing nothing in political information.
Even in a close election the chance that one vote decides the result is effectively zero, so expected gains from voting are near zero.

definition.text: A research programme that applies public choice and political economy to the design of constitutional rules.

facts.text: Buchanan and Tullock argued that for government to benefit everyone, people must agree on the rules, not on every government action.
They split decisions into constitutional ones, which set lasting rules, and political ones made within those rules.
